claims.text: A DNN potential trained on ab initio data can accurately and efficiently predict melting temperatures across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The approach can determine enthalpy and entropy of fusion and volume change at melting across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The approach can determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
Combining molecular dynamics and thermodynamic integration with a DNN potential captures effects of local atomic configuration and nonideal mixing on phase transitions.
High-entropy carbides and oxides can occur as single-phase multicomponent solid solutions.
The proposed DNN potential is trained on DFT data.
Thermodynamic integration can be performed over the solid-to-liquid transition across a range of compositions using this potential.
Laser melting and differential thermal analysis can validate the DNN-based predictions.
The method is applicable to refractory alloys and systems with similar bonding characteristics.
Atomistic pair correlations and local structural ordering can be quantified during DNN-potential simulations.
Pair correlations and local structural ordering mediate the changes in enthalpy, entropy, and volume upon melting.
Nonideal mixing in solid and liquid phases changes local bonding and configurational entropy.
Accurately representing these interactions enables thermodynamic integration to determine latent heat, melting-temperature shifts, and volume changes.
Increasing nitrogen content in high-entropy carbonitrides increases melting temperature nonlinearly, with a maximum near 25% nitrogen.
Predicted melting temperatures should agree with experiment within approximately ±30 K.
Predicted enthalpy, entropy, and volume changes at melting should agree with measurements within approximately ±5%.
The cited literature provides experimental laser-melting and differential-thermal-analysis baselines for high-entropy materials.
The method is likely robust for single-phase refractory solid solutions but may not transfer to phase-segregated, extremely disordered, or differently bonded systems.
Transferability over broad composition space and treatment of rare events or structural transitions remain uncertain.
Consistent errors exceeding ±30 K in melting temperature or ±5% in latent heat or volume change across multiple compositions would falsify the proposed accuracy claim.
